core: What an essay is: a multi-paragraph piece of writing that develops one central argument or thesis
The thesis statement: the essay's main claim, typically one sentence near the end of the introduction; what makes it strong (specific, arguable, supportable)
Essay structure: introduction with hook and thesis; body paragraphs each with their own topic sentence; conclusion that synthesizes
Types of essays named briefly: argumentative, expository, descriptive, narrative
The writing process: prewriting/brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, editing, proofreading

claims.claim: An essay is a multi-paragraph piece of writing that develops a single central idea — the thesis — and the thesis statement summarizes the entire essay the way a topic sentence summarizes one paragraph.

A strong thesis statement is specific, precise, and arguable: it states a position that can be supported with evidence, rather than announcing the topic, stating an obvious fact, or relying on phrases like 'I believe'.
The thesis statement most often appears near the end of the introduction; the introduction first captures the reader's interest with an engaging opening (the hook) and introduces the topic.

Each body paragraph develops one point that supports the thesis, is controlled by its own topic sentence, and is supported by specific details, examples, or evidence; essays commonly have at least three body paragraphs.
The conclusion paraphrases the thesis, reviews the essay's main points, and closes the essay without introducing new material or contradicting the thesis.

The classic writing process stages are prewriting (brainstorming), outlining, drafting, revising, editing, and proofreading; writers move back and forth among stages as the draft requires (the process is recursive).

Revising improves the ideas of a draft (adding, cutting, moving, changing content), editing improves expression (word choice, grammar, punctuation, sentence structure), and proofreading catches surface errors such as spelling and capitalization.
Transitions are words and phrases that show how the ideas in sentences and paragraphs are related; adding them is a practical fix for an essay that jumps abruptly between points.

Common academic essay types include argumentative (persuading readers toward a point of view), expository (explaining or informing), descriptive (creating a vivid picture through sensory detail), and narrative (telling a story); the writer's purpose determines the type.

Body paragraphs must relate directly to the thesis; supporting material that does not connect to the main claim should be cut, and each paragraph's relevance can be checked against its topic sentence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How long is a thesis statement?
positions: Writing for Success: 'A thesis is one sentence long and appears toward the end of your introduction.'

Purdue OWL (citing the MLA Handbook): 'A thesis statement is a single sentence that formulates both your topic and your point of view,' while noting complex papers may require a combination of sentences.
OpenStax Writing Guide: a thesis is a 'declarative sentence (sometimes two) that states a writer's position.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the thesis as a sentence (sometimes two) that states the essay's main claim; the single-sentence form is the norm, with longer theses acceptable for complex papers.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many body paragraphs should an essay have?
positions: Writing for Success: at least three body paragraphs is the common expectation, and the five-paragraph essay is standard for exams and essay assignments.
Purdue OWL: essay structure is 'guidelines' that must stay flexible enough for the purpose and audience.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says essays commonly have at least three body paragraphs — one per major point — without presenting the five-paragraph form as a universal rule.

sourceRecords.provider: Saylor Academy (adapted from University of Minnesota Libraries' Writing for Success)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 via HTTPS. Supports: body paragraphs follow the path set by the thesis; each body paragraph contains a topic sentence stating one aspect of the thesis plus supporting details; primary support must be specific, detailed, and relevant to the thesis; unrelated ideas should be omitted; at least three body paragraphs is the common expectation. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Writing Introductory and Concluding Paragraphs — Writing for Success
sourceRecords.provider: Saylor Academy (adapted from University of Minnesota Libraries' Writing for Success)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 via HTTPS. Supports: introduction engages readers immediately (provocative question, startling statistic, quotation, anecdote, striking image), introduces the topic, and states the thesis — often via the funnel technique of narrowing from general to specific; strong conclusion restates/paraphrases the thesis, reviews main points, and closes with an emphatic statement; conclusions should avoid new material, contradicting the thesis, and apologies. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Rhetorical Modes — Writing for Success
sourceRecords.provider: Saylor Academy (adapted from University of Minnesota Libraries' Writing for Success)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 via HTTPS. Supports the essay types: the rhetorical mode a writer chooses depends on purpose; narration is the art of storytelling that emotionally engages the reader (with a strong introduction to hook the reader and sensory details); description uses the five senses; persuasion is the attempt to convince or move readers toward a certain point of view. Expository patterns in the same chapter (illustration, classification, process analysis, definition, comparison and contrast, cause and effect) support the one-line characterization of expository essays as explaining or informing. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Argument Papers: Body Paragraphs — Purdue OWL
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: body paragraphs move from general to specific information; the four elements of a good paragraph are transition, topic sentence, specific evidence and analysis, and a brief wrap-up (warrant) that connects the paragraph back to the thesis; a topic sentence tells the reader what the paragraph will discuss. Reference only.
